title: The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), concert overture
hook: A seascape in sound, whose opening came to Mendelssohn on a Scottish island and went straight into a letter home.

painting.title: Staffa, Fingal’s Cave
painting.collection: Yale Center for British Art, New Haven
painting.pairingNote: Turner sailed to Staffa in 1831, two years after Mendelssohn, and showed this stormy view of the island at the Royal Academy in 1832, the year the overture was first played in London.

facts: In the summer of 1829 Mendelssohn, aged twenty, toured Scotland on foot with his friend Karl Klingemann. On 7 August they reached Tobermory on the Isle of Mull, and that evening he wrote home to show “how extraordinarily the Hebrides have affected me”. In the letter he sketched what had come into his head there: the first twenty-one bars of the overture, already with notes on which instruments should play.

The next day the two friends sailed to the small island of Staffa to see Fingal’s Cave, a sea cave lined with black basalt columns. Mendelssohn was too seasick to write; Klingemann described a cave like the inside of an enormous organ, full of the roar of the waves. So the famous opening was written before Mendelssohn ever saw the cave.

He finished a first version in Rome on 16 December 1830, calling it *The Lonely Island*, then revised it heavily. The new version was first played in London on 14 May 1832, and it was published in 1833–35 under several titles: *The Hebrides* on the parts, *Fingal’s Cave* on the score.

It is a concert overture: a single piece for the concert hall, not the prelude to a play or an opera. It tells no story but paints a mood, and some count it among the first tone poems. Wagner called Mendelssohn “a landscape painter of the first order”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a rolling sea, a broad song for the cellos, storms and calm, and a quiet ending on the waves.

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: One movement in [[sonata-form|sonata form]]. A short, rocking phrase, low in the orchestra, is repeated again and again like waves; a broad, singing second theme in the cellos and bassoons answers it. The middle grows stormy, the themes return, a fast burst near the end whips up the sea once more, and the overture ends quietly, as if the island were disappearing from view.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a short phrase that rises and falls, played softly in the violas, cellos and bassoons and repeated on different notes, like waves rolling in.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a long, warm melody in D major, first in the cellos and bassoons, one of Mendelssohn’s best-loved tunes.

mainIdeas.name: The calls
mainIdeas.description: short fanfares in the woodwinds and brass, like voices or signals heard across the water.

stops.hear: Low, soft strings and bassoons play a short rocking phrase, over and over, rising and falling
stops.happening: Theme 1, the sketch in the letter of 7 August 1829

stops.hear: The same phrase climbs higher; the whole orchestra swells and settles
A broad, warm melody, sung by the cellos and bassoons
Bright calls in the woodwinds and trumpets; the music gathers strength
Quieter: the opening phrase passed between instruments, wandering into new keys
The sea rises: loud, rushing strings and heavy brass
stops.happening: The storm, the climax of the development

stops.hear: The rocking opening phrase returns in the home key
The broad second melody again, now in the clarinets
Suddenly faster and louder: a new burst of energy across the whole orchestra
Calm again: a clarinet sings a last echo of the second theme

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Soft wisps of the opening phrase and a few plucked notes; then silence

notice: Listen to the very beginning: the rocking phrase almost never stops. It is the sea under everything else.
Notice how quietly the overture ends. After all the storms, there is no loud final chord.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Claudio Abbado was principal conductor of the London Symphony Orchestra when he recorded all of Mendelssohn’s symphonies and overtures with it for Deutsche Grammophon in the mid-1980s.

threads.title: A picture in sound
threads.body: The overture describes no events, only a place and a mood. Later composers would call such pieces [[symphonic-poem|symphonic poems]]; Mendelssohn called it an overture.

threads.title: Scotland
threads.body: The same journey of 1829 also gave Mendelssohn the first idea for his *Scottish* Symphony, which he finished only thirteen years later.

threads.title: Revisions
threads.body: Mendelssohn kept rewriting his music. He reworked this overture several times between 1830 and 1832 before letting it be published, and the opening sketch from the letter survived almost unchanged.
